answer: Hi, I’m Leaffy, SoilSync’s little leaf companion! I can help with the SoilSync project, food scraps, home composting and beginner gardening. What would you like to explore?

SoilSync is TEDA BYTE’s Food Waste & Home Gardening Companion, a capstone prototype for residential households. It helps you identify food scraps, learn home composting, care for a small garden and build greener daily habits.

Log in or register, then photograph scraps in Snap Waste. Review the identification and choose a suitable recipe. Create separate named batches and follow their three photo check-ins. If live AI is unavailable, retry later; no scan result or points are invented.

Daily check-in earns 10 EcoPoints, a new scan with compostable waste earns 50, and an approved weekly batch quest earns 100. Chat earns no points. Duplicate scans and repeated check-ins do not award points again.

Browse Rewards for the current items and point costs. Coffee offers, eco-bags and seeds are project reward concepts. Claims do not issue a real voucher or arrange collection; partner fulfilment is not connected.

The online app uses server-side Google Gemini for waste recognition, compost-photo checks and Leaffy chat. Internet is required for live AI. Your laptop and USB cable are not needed by the installed online APK. My bundled project guide can answer some questions when live AI is unavailable.

Your account, batches and reward claims are stored in PostgreSQL. Scan and weekly proof photos go to Google Gemini for analysis. Approved weekly proof photos are stored privately and only their owner can view them. Chat questions go to Gemini; this app keeps the conversation in screen memory until you leave or clear it.

The current online SoilSync app uses React, Vite and Capacitor with a FastAPI backend on Vercel, Google Gemini and a shared Neon PostgreSQL database. pgAdmin is a tool for viewing and editing a connected database. Firebase also hosts a separate trainer demo.

SoilSync is a TEDA BYTE capstone project. Its focus is household food waste and home gardening. I don’t have verified individual team roles, sponsor agreements or project assessment details in my guide, so I won’t invent them.

A photo is a starting point for identifying scraps; review and correct the result when needed. SoilSync cannot measure nutrients, contamination, pathogens or compost maturity from an image. The current household UI does not provide collection operators, verified handovers, lab telemetry or bioreactors.

For a wet or smelly beginner compost pile, add dry browns such as plain shredded cardboard or dry leaves. Mix gently for airflow, and pause wet additions until the balance improves. Aim for dampness like a wrung-out sponge.

If your compost is too dry, add water gradually and mix. Aim for dampness like a wrung-out sponge, with airflow. Break suitable scraps into smaller pieces and keep greens balanced with dry browns. There is no guaranteed completion date.

Fruit peels, vegetable trimmings and cooled coffee grounds can suit beginner home composting. Remove packaging and stickers, chop larger scraps and mix with dry browns. Crush eggshells; they break down slowly. Keep meat, fish, bones, dairy and oily foods out of a beginner pile.

Use finished, earthy-smelling compost with no recognisable scraps as a soil amendment, rather than pure potting soil. Never put fresh scraps directly against roots. Herbs or leafy greens in pots with drainage can be a starting point; check the chosen plant’s sunlight and watering needs.
